On Being Asked to Write Freely

There is a strange and wonderful permission in being told to "write freely about whatever you want." No prompt, no boundaries, no rubric. Just space. White space that suddenly feels heavier than any assignment ever did. Most writing we do in life is responsive — we answer a question, we reply to an email, we fill out a form, we argue a point someone else has made. But to be told, simply, *go* — to be handed 2500 words of blank land and told to build whatever you like — is both exhilarating and slightly terrifying. It's like being left alone in an enormous library after hours with a flashlight. Where do you even point it first?

So I will point it at a few things I have been thinking about for a long time, things that don't quite fit together but keep orbiting each other in my mind anyway: attention, time, small things, unfinished things, and the quiet, stubborn human desire to make meaning out of all of it.

Let's start with attention, because attention is where everything else starts.

### 1. The Currency We Spend Without Noticing

We talk a lot about time as our most valuable resource, but that isn't quite right. Time passes whether we spend it well or not. Attention is the real currency. Time is just the riverbed; attention is the water. And right now, we live in an economy explicitly designed to dam, divert, and siphon that water as efficiently as possible.

A hundred years ago, if you wanted to be distracted, you had to work for it. You had to go somewhere, buy something, find someone. Boredom was the default state, and stimulation was the exception. Now it's inverted. Stimulation is the default — an infinite, frictionless feed — and sustained attention is the thing you have to work for. You have to build walls around it.

I don't say this as a moral panic. I'm not here to tell you phones are ruining us, because the truth is more nuanced. The devices in our pockets have also given us access to more art, more knowledge, more human connection than any generation before us could have imagined. I can read a letter that Seneca wrote to his friend Lucilius 2,000 years ago while waiting for my coffee. I can watch a falcon hatch live in the Scottish Highlands. That is a kind of miracle.

But the trade is real. The system that delivers those miracles is funded by keeping our eyes from lingering too long on any one thing. The ideal user, from the platform's perspective, is not a person who reads one article deeply and sits with it for an afternoon. The ideal user is a person who skims twenty articles shallowly and clicks to the next thing. The architecture rewards that.

So the radical act, now, is not to consume more. It's to linger.

To read the same poem three times in a row. To watch the same tree for ten minutes and notice how the light moves through it. To have a conversation without checking to see if anything more interesting is happening elsewhere. To let your attention be inefficient.

We have started to treat efficiency as the highest virtue, but attention is valuable precisely because it is inefficient. Love is inefficient. Wonder is inefficient. Grief is inefficient. If you try to optimize them, you destroy them.

I have been trying to practice what the writer Mary Oliver called "attention as prayer." She wrote, "Attention is the beginning of devotion." Not attention as a productivity hack, but attention as a way of saying: *this matters. I am here for this.* For five minutes, for an hour, I will not be anywhere else.

It is harder than it sounds. The mind is a restless animal. It wants to dart. But every time I manage to actually pay attention — to really listen to a friend, to really taste food, to really look at the sky until I can see its color changing — I am reminded that this is not a luxury. This is the substance of a life.

### 2. Deep Time and the Human Scale

Once, in a museum in Utah, I stood in front of a slab of rock with a fossilized fern pressed into it. The placard said it was 310 million years old. I did the math in my head and immediately failed to comprehend it. 310 million years is not a number a human brain is built to hold. We are built to hold maybe eighty years, if we're lucky. Maybe we can stretch to imagine our grandparents' childhoods, or our grandchildren's old age. Beyond that, it becomes abstraction.

But standing there, I tried anyway. I tried to imagine the fern when it was alive, unfurling in a swamp where dragonflies the size of hawks buzzed through warm, oxygen-rich air. There were no humans. There were no mammals. There were no flowers. Dinosaurs wouldn't appear for another 80 million years. The continent I was standing on was unrecognizable, smashed together with others into a different shape.

And somehow that tiny, delicate imprint had survived everything — continental drift, ice ages, asteroid impacts, the rise and fall of entire kingdoms of life — so that I, a primate who evolved yesterday by geological standards, could stand in an air-conditioned room and look at it.

Geologists call this "deep time," a term that was first truly grasped only a couple hundred years ago. Before that, most people in the Western world believed the Earth was a few thousand years old. The discovery that it was actually billions of years old was one of the most profound psychological displacements in human history, as dizzying in its own way as discovering that the Earth was not the center of the universe.

Deep time does something strange to you. At first, it makes you feel insignificant. What is one human life against 4.5 billion years? But if you sit with it a little longer, it does the opposite. It makes everything feel incredibly precious and improbable. That you are here at all, that consciousness arose in the universe and turned around to look at itself, that we can *know* about the fern and the dragonflies — that is astonishing.

We live on two clocks at once. There's the human clock: deadlines, birthdays, heartbeats, the quick succession of days that feels so urgent. And there's the geological clock: the slow grinding of mountains into dust, the wandering of stars. We need both. If we live only on the human clock, we become anxious and myopic. If we live only on the geological clock, we become detached and fatalistic. Wisdom is learning to hear both ticks at once.

I like to think about this when I get stuck in traffic or anxious about an email I sent. I picture the fern. I picture the rock. Not to minimize my own worries — they are real at their scale — but to put them in context. This moment is both tiny and huge. Both. At the same time.

### 3. The Library of Unfinished Things

Everyone carries around an invisible library. Not the library of books we've read, but the library of things we've started and not finished. The novel half-written in a drawer. The language we learned for three weeks on an app. The garden we planned but never planted. The apology we rehearsed but never delivered. The person we intended to become when we were twelve.

We tend to treat these unfinished things with shame, as evidence of our failure to follow through. But I have come to think they deserve more tenderness than that.

An unfinished thing is not necessarily a failure. Sometimes it's a record of who you were when you started it. The half-knitted scarf from when you thought you wanted to be someone who knits. The abandoned research project from when you were fascinated by octopuses. They are artifacts of past selves, and past selves deserve to be archived, not scolded.

The Japanese have a concept called *tsundoku* — the act of buying books and letting them pile up unread. It's often treated as a slightly guilty habit, but there is also a beautiful idea hidden in it: that the unread books are not a to-do list, but a field of possibility. The scholar Nassim Taleb takes this further with his idea of the "antilibrary" — that our unread books are more valuable than our read ones, because they remind us of what we don't know. They keep us humble and curious.

I think we need an antilibrary for our whole lives. A room where we keep the drafts without needing to publish them, the hobbies without needing to monetize them, the curiosities without needing to make them productive. A place where we allow things to be unfinished because the process was worthwhile, even if the product never arrived.

One of my favorite stories is about Leonardo da Vinci. We think of him as the ultimate genius-finisher, but he was in fact a notorious non-finisher. He left paintings incomplete for years, abandoning them to chase an anatomy study or a design for a flying machine that would never fly. His notebooks are full of to-do lists that veer from the sublime to the mundane: "calculate the measurement of Milan and its suburbs," "ask Benedetto Portinari by what means they go on ice in Flanders," "describe the tongue of the woodpecker." He never finished most of what he started. But the unfinishedness *was* the work. The wandering was the point.

Maybe we should be less obsessed with finishing and more obsessed with starting with wholehearted curiosity. Maybe a life well-lived is not a tidy bibliography of completed projects, but a sprawling, dusty studio full of half-sculptures, sketches, and beautiful questions.

What unfinished thing are you carrying that you could forgive yourself for? What if you let it just be what it was — a season of interest — and put it gently on the shelf?

### 4. The Physics of Small Things

We are taught to look for importance in scale. Big discoveries, big movements, big histories. But the universe is often most eloquent in small things.

Take dust. Household dust, the stuff you wipe off your shelf and never think about again. Most of it is not actually "dirt from outside" the way we imagine. A significant fraction of it is you. Skin cells, hair fragments, fibers from your clothes. And also: tiny fragments of meteorites. Every year, about 40,000 tons of cosmic dust falls to Earth — pulverized asteroids and comet tails that have been drifting through space for billions of years, finally slowing enough to be caught by our atmosphere and settle, invisibly, on your windowsill. When you wipe dust away, you are, in a literal sense, wiping away stardust.

Or take mycelium, the underground fungal network that connects forests. A single cubic inch of healthy soil can contain eight miles of fungal hyphae — threads thinner than human hair. Trees use this network to share nutrients and even information. A dying tree will send its remaining sugars through the mycelium to its neighbors. A mother tree will nourish its shaded seedlings. Scientists call it the "Wood Wide Web," which is a cute name, but it undersells how strange and profound it is: the forest is not a collection of individuals competing, but a community negotiating, sharing, remembering.

Or take a bee. A honeybee weighs about a tenth of a gram. Its brain is the size of a grass seed and contains about a million neurons — compared to our 86 billion. And yet a bee can learn to recognize human faces, understand the concept of zero — a concept human children don't grasp until around age four — and communicate the precise location of flowers to its hivemates through a dance that encodes angle relative to the sun and distance. Small body, enormous competence.

We overlook small things because our eyes are calibrated for predators and prey at our own scale. But if you train yourself to crouch down — literally and metaphorically — the world becomes incredibly dense with wonder. The lichen on a rock, which is not one organism but two — a fungus and an alga living together so intimately they were thought to be a single plant for a century. The way water beads on a leaf because of microscopic wax crystals. The fact that your fingernails and a rhinoceros horn are made of the same protein.

Attention, again. The world is always broadcasting. We just have to tune to the right frequency.

I keep a magnifying glass in my bag. Not for any practical reason — I don't have particularly bad eyesight. I keep it because it reminds me to look closer. People laugh when they see it, but when I hand it to them and point to the edge of a leaf or the weave of their shirt, they always gasp a little. "I didn't know it looked like that." It's all there, all the time. We just walk past it.

### 5. The Future Is Not a Place We Are Going, But a Place We Are Making

We tend to talk about the future as if it is a distant destination we are traveling toward — like a science-fiction city we will one day arrive at. But the future isn't a place. It's a consequence. It's the sum of the choices we make, and don't make, right now.

For a long time, the dominant story about the future was one of inevitable progress: things will get better, technology will solve our problems, the arc will bend toward justice on its own. That story has cracked. Now the dominant story for many people is one of inevitable collapse: climate change will make the planet uninhabitable, inequality will spiral, artificial intelligence will outwit us. Both stories share the same fatalism: the future is something that will *happen to us*.

But neither story is true. The future is not inevitable. It is made.

And it is made mostly not by grand, cinematic moments, but by boring, incremental, unglamorous decisions. By the city council that decides to build a bike lane. By the teacher who stays late to help a kid who is about to drop out. By the engineer who chooses to make an algorithm more interpretable even though it's less profitable. By the neighbor who plants a tree whose shade she will never sit in.

Anthropologists talk about the "seven-generation principle" practiced by some Indigenous nations — the idea that decisions should be made with consideration for seven generations ahead. In a world oriented around quarterly earnings and 24-hour news cycles, that kind of thinking feels almost alien. But it is perhaps the most practical mindset we could adopt.

What would it mean to live as good ancestors? To ask, before we act: what will this look like to someone born in 2125? Will they be grateful we did this? Will they wish we hadn't? Will they even know we existed?

This is not about guilt. It's about imagination. The future needs more imagination, not less. We are suffering, in many ways, from a failure of imagination. We can imagine dystopias in vivid, high-definition detail — we've watched dozens of them in movies — but we struggle to imagine a plausible, thriving world in the year 2070. What does a carbon-negative city look like? What does an economy that values care work look like? What does a healthy relationship with technology look like? We need artists and writers and kids and engineers to paint those pictures for us, because we cannot build what we cannot imagine.

One of my favorite recent ideas is the concept of "long-term art." There is a project in Norway called the Future Library. Every year, an author contributes a manuscript that will remain unread, sealed, until the year 2114. The paper to print the books is being grown right now — a forest was planted outside Oslo in 2014 that will supply the paper a century from now. No one alive today who started the project will see its end. It is an act of pure trust in the future. It says: we believe there will still be humans, there will still be readers, there will still be forests and books. That belief itself helps bring that future into being.

We write the future with our actions, but also with our beliefs about it. Hope is not naive optimism. Hope is a discipline. It's a decision to act as if the future is worth fighting for, even when you aren't sure it is. Especially then.

### Epilogue: So, What Now?

If you have read this far, thank you for spending a piece of your finite attention here with me. I know there were a thousand other things you could have skimmed instead.

I don't have a neat conclusion for all of this. I didn't start with a thesis to prove; I started with a flashlight and a library. If there is a thread that ties these wandering thoughts together, it is probably this: that meaning is not something you find, fully formed, like a coin on the sidewalk. It's something you *make* by looking closely, by lingering, by remembering your scale in the universe and choosing to act with care anyway.

So, if you want a small, practical experiment to take from this very long, very free piece of writing, try this:

Tomorrow, pick one small thing — a mug, a crack in the sidewalk, the sound of your refrigerator humming — and give it sixty seconds of uninterrupted attention. No photo, no note, no goal. Just look or listen. Notice its texture, its history, its tiny physics. Let it be enough.

Then, maybe, pick one unfinished thing in your inner library and forgive it. Or pick one future-oriented action, however small — an email, a donation, planting something — and do it as a gift to someone seven generations from now who will never know your name.

That is how we write freely, after all. Not just with words, but with days.

We fill the blank pages we were given as best we can, knowing the story will remain unfinished, knowing most of it will become dust eventually, and doing it anyway — with as much attention, tenderness, and wonder as we can muster.

There is no final draft. There is only the ongoing draft. And that, I think, is more than enough.
